headline: GPT-6.1 Terra is cheapest LLM for 77-intent banking classification at $0.000727
summary: GPT-6.1 Terra achieved an 84.0% pass rate on 150 BANKING77 messages, matching the baseline GPT-6.1 Sol for 42.8% less cost per successful task.
details: GPT-6.1 Terra has been identified as the most cost-effective LLM for 77-intent banking classification, clearing a 70% pass bar and matching the baseline GPT-6.1 Sol. It costs $0.000727 per successful task, a 42.8% reduction compared to Sol's $0.001272.

While other models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 are cheaper per task, they do not statistically match the baseline's performance. Luna passes 82.0% at $0.00009, and Haiku 5.5 passes 80.0% at $0.000138 with the lowest latency.

The evaluation involved 150 messages from the BANKING77 test split, requiring models to reply with a single intent label from a 77-label list. Models were allowed up to two retries for invalid labels, with all attempts' costs counted.

The study highlights that raw token prices can be misleading due to retries. Models like deepseek-v4.1-flash and mistral-large-4 incurred significant costs from retries, with mistral-large-4 spending 44.6% of its budget on retries.

The definition of 'clears the bar' (lower end of 95% Wilson interval at or above 70%) differs from 'matches the baseline' (no more than 5 points worse than baseline in a paired test). This distinction is crucial for accurate model selection.

The full dataset, prompt, prices, and re-run script are available on the verdict page, allowing users to replicate the comparison with their own OpenRouter key. Prices are noted as of 2026-11-05 and are subject to monthly changes.

A tool is available during early access for users to import their own input/expected pairs and current model. It identifies the cheapest model that clears their specific performance bar, providing cost per successful task and detailing failures.

headline: OpenAI drops NDAs with public officials for new data center projects
summary: This move is part of new community commitments for its 'compute campuses,' addressing public opposition to data center expansion and increasing transparency with local officials.
details: OpenAI has announced it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials involved in its data center projects. This decision comes amidst growing public opposition to data center expansion, as voiced in recent midterms. It marks a significant shift towards greater transparency in its "compute campus" developments.

Previously, many data center projects faced scrutiny for relying on NDAs to obscure discussions between developers and local authorities. OpenAI now states it will permit "only narrow protections" for legitimate security, trade secrets, or competitively sensitive information. This aligns with Amazon's similar announcement in October regarding NDAs with government agencies.

The company's new commitments also include covering the full cost of electricity and necessary infrastructure for its operations. OpenAI will publish expected job creation figures and report on local hiring opportunities. Each future "compute campus" will feature a "local compact" incorporating these commitments and reflecting community priorities.
